an2.11:1.6: This links back to [an2.1](). Here, “reflection” (_paṭisaṅkhā_) is the wisdom of a thoughtful examination of one’s life and choices, which manifests as a genuine change in behavior.
an2.11:2.2: The “trainees” are at least stream-enterers, having realized the four noble truths. The path has already manifested in them, so their task is to “develop” it (_bhāvanā_), literally, “make it be more, amplify”.
an2.12:2.1: The text introduces the seven “awakening factors”, which especially emphasize the emotional and holistic dimension of meditative growth. Unlike the eightfold path, they do not explicitly include the factor of ethics, but such passages as [sn46.1:1.4]() show that ethics is their foundation. | Here the text does not specify that it applies to trainees only. A trainee undertakes “development” in the purest sense of amplifying spiritual qualities that are already present, whereas those practicing for stream-entry are establishing those same qualities.
an2.12:2.2: The factors of mindfulness and investigation of principles both have a dual meaning in this context. They can refer to “bringing to mind” and “investigating” the principles or phenomena experienced in meditation. But they can also refer to recalling the “teaching” and reflecting on it ([sn46.3]()).
an2.12:2.3: This is the same practice that is referred to as “reflection” above. | _Dhamma_ here means the “principle” of cause and effect, as in “observation of principles” (_dhammānupassanā_), “investigation of principles” (_dhammavicaya_), or “discernment of principles” (_dhammavipassanā_).
an2.12:2.4: Energy has been emphasized in the previous chapter.
an2.12:2.5: “Rapture” (_pīti_) is a joyous emotional response to pleasure, usually a spiritual sense of elevation or uplift in meditation.
an2.12:2.6: “Tranquility” (_passaddhi_) is a settled and serene body and mind, as activities or energies become stilled through the process of meditation.
an2.12:2.7: “Immersion” (_samādhi_) is equivalent to the four absorptions, which is why the passage of the seven awakening factors parallels the four absorptions in the next discourse.
an2.12:2.8: “Equanimity” (_upekkhā_) of the fourth absorption and above, or else the equanimity of insight ([mn152]()).
an2.13:2.2: “Absorption” (_jhāna_) is a state of “elevated consciousness” (_adhicitta_), so all the terms have an elevated sense; for more details, see the notes to [dn2:75.1](). | The plural form indicates that “sensual pleasures” includes sense experience, which the meditator can turn away from since they no longer have any desire for it. | The “unskillful qualities” are the five hindrances. | The “rapture and bliss born of seclusion” is the happiness of abandoning the hindrances and freedom from sense impingement. | “Placing the mind and keeping it connected” (_vitakka_, _vicāra_) uses terms that mean “thought” in coarse consciousness, but which in “elevated consciousness” refer to the subtle function of applying the mind to the meditation.
an2.13:2.3: Each _jhāna_ begins as the least refined aspect of the previous _jhāna_ ends. This is not consciously directed, but describes the natural process of settling. The meditator is now fully confident and no longer needs to apply their mind: it is simply still and fully unified.
an2.13:2.4: The emotional response to bliss matures from the subtle thrill of rapture to the poise of equanimity. Mindfulness is present in all states of deep meditation, but with equanimity it becomes prominent.
an2.13:2.5: The emotional poise of equanimity leads to the feeling of pleasure settling into the more subtle neutral feeling. Pain and sadness have been abandoned long before, but are emphasized here as they are subtle counterpart of pleasure.
an2.14:1.3: At [sn36.19](), two students of the Buddha debate whether the Buddha taught two feelings or three. The Buddha explains that he taught both ways, and many more besides. Thus understanding that there are different modes of exposition helps avoid conflict and confusion.
an2.14:1.4: This principle is important for those of us who try to uncover the historical process of text formation. As a rule, Buddhist texts tend to get longer over time; it seems Buddhists were more apt to add things to make them clearer or more appealing, rather than removing things that they considered the Buddha’s words. Nevertheless, we cannot assume that something is later just because it is longer, since the Buddha (or his disciples) might teach the same thing in longer and shorter versions at different occasions. This is why, when assessing the provenance of a text, we look for multiple independent criteria: length is one factor, but also terminology, style, doctrine, historical cues, parallels in other languages, and so on. The capacity of text historical criticism should not be overestimated, as we find clear indications in only a small portion of texts.
an2.15:1.1: This discourse lends the chapter its name. While the topic of monastic disciplinary issues is new, the monastics “check” (_paccavekkhati_) themselves as they “reflect” above.
an2.15:1.4: The Vinaya does not assume that monastics are perfect, but it does rely on them having integrity and a capacity for self-reflection.
an2.15:2.3: This process is further described at [an10.23]().
an2.15:2.11: _Suṅka_ (Sanskrit _śulka_) is a “fee”, which may be a dowry, but here means “customs duty”. Customs duty was a significant source of revenue for governments, and evasion was considered a form of theft for monastics ([pli-tv-bu-vb-pj2:4.21.2]()). Kauṭilya discusses the administration of customs in detail at Arthaśāstra 2.21.1.
an2.16:1.1: This is the first interreligious dialogue in the Aṅguttara, and the first conversion narrative. | The brahmins were members of a hereditary caste descended from the poets and priests of the Vedas, who were entrusted with the maintenance of Vedic traditions and texts, and performance of Vedic rites. They believed they were the superior representatives of Divinity in the mortal realm. They had diverse lifestyles as householders, landowners, farmers, royal advisers, soothsayers, renunciants, or wanderers. The religion of the brahmins was undergoing profound changes as the ritualism of the Vedas was deepened and challenged through the contemplative philosophies of the Upaniṣads, which the Buddha studied and practiced before his awakening. It was to evolve for another thousands years, absorbing much Buddhist influence, before reaching the full-fledged synthesis that today we call Hinduism.
an2.16:1.3: There is a set of beliefs about hell that is common to Buddhists, Hindus, and Jains. This “hell complex” includes such beliefs as: hell is long-lasting but impermanent; there are many named hells; punishments are terrible and varied; the punishment is determined by kamma; and tortures are inflicted by hell wardens. For details and Brahmanical parallels, see [mn130]() and notes.
an2.16:1.4: While contemporary Vedic texts are not explicit, later Hinduism had to negotiate the question whether good rebirth was due to performance of rituals or ethical conduct, comparable to the tension between faith and works in Christianity. This is why even learned brahmins, like the learned doctors of the Christian faiths, debated a matter that seems simple to a Buddhist: rebirth is determined by actions.
an2.17:1.1: We meet Jānussoṇi many times in the suttas, where he converses with the Buddha on a number of topics, with a special interest in the afterlife. His name appears in Sanskrit as Jānaśruti or Jānaśruteya, which are patronymics of Janaśruti, “famed among the people”, with the element _soṇi_ coming from the Vedic _ṣvaṇi_ (“sound”). The Chinese rendering 生聞 (“Born Famous”, T 125.2.665b18) evidently assumes the same derivation (_jana_ “people” is from √_jan_ “born”). The Pali commentary says it is a title awarded the family priest (_purohita_) of Kosala, which would make him one of the most powerful brahmins alive. However, I can find no confirmation of such a title, whereas the use of Jānaśruti as a patronymic by the descendants of Janaśruti is well attested. One such, perhaps the same individual we meet in the Suttas, features in Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.1–3 as a generous seeker of the truth.
an2.17:3.1: Jānussoṇi goes for refuge so often in the suttas that it is almost a genre unto itself ([mn4](), [mn27](), [sn12.47](), [an3.55](), [an3.59](), [an4.184](), [an6.52](), [an7.47](), [an10.119](), [an10.167](), [an10.177]()). Such narrative accounts of conversion or enlightenment at the end of discourses are not very reliable, as they are not the Buddha’s words but were added by editors at some point.
an2.19:1.10: This essential encouragement shows the Buddha’s faith in human potential rather than divine salvation.
an2.20:1.3: This harks back to [an2.14]() as they both deal with texts.
